title: The Schedule Is a Model of Logic, Not a List of Dates
summary: Petra builds a small critical path network, runs the forward and backward pass, and shows how float measures the slack before the finish moves. She explains who can own float, why a baseline must be reviewed for logic before acceptance, and how look-aheads and the Last Planner System turn the plan into weekly commitments.
body:
A schedule is not a list of dates. It is a model of logic: which work must finish before which other work can start. Get the logic right and the dates, the critical path and the float follow; get it wrong and every date on the page is a guess in a neat font.

Recall

Q. What is a change directive?

A. A written instruction from the owner to proceed with a change before price and time are agreed, valued later by a method the contract states, with cost records kept.

Q. What is the owner decision log, and which two columns matter most?

A. The single record of every owner decision. Date needed, which shows the owner's own delay as a risk, and authority, which proves the decision was made by someone allowed to make it.

Q. What is a special purpose vehicle in project finance?

A. A company created to own one project, so that its assets, debts and contracts are separated from the sponsor's other business and lenders can look to the project's cash flows.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, last week we defined what is being built. This week Petra, our scheduling lead, defines when. Time is the variable that connects everything else in this phase: the loan's maturity, the interest reserve, the lease-up, the contractor's overheads and your own equity. You met the daily cost of a project in Week 48. Today you learn the tool that tells you which days actually cost money, and which can slip for free.

Your control-room background is a real advantage here. A switching sequence is a dependency chain: this breaker cannot close until that isolator is open. A construction schedule is the same thing, at a much larger scale.

The critical path method: logic first

In plain English, the critical path method builds a network of activities, each with a duration, linked by the order in which they must happen, and then finds the longest chain through the network. That longest chain decides the finish date.

The professional term is the critical path method (CPM), developed in the late 1950s for large industrial projects and now the basis of almost every construction schedule. Each link is a logic relationship, most often finish-to-start: activity B cannot start until activity A finishes. Other types exist, start-to-start and finish-to-finish, sometimes with a lag, a waiting time between the linked activities.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers in working days. Four activities. A, excavation, 10 days. B, foundations, 15 days, after A. C, underground utilities, 8 days, also after A. D, ground-floor slab, 20 days, after both B and C. Now the forward pass, which finds the earliest each activity can start and finish. A runs days 0 to 10. B runs 10 to 25. C runs 10 to 18. D cannot start until both B and C are done, so it starts at day 25 and finishes at day 45. The project takes 45 days.

Then the backward pass, which finds the latest each activity can finish without delaying the end. D must finish by 45, so it must start by 25. B must finish by 25, so it must start by 10. C must also finish by 25, so it may start as late as day 17. A must finish by 10.

Float: the slack in the network

In plain English, float is how long an activity can slip before it delays the finish date.

Total float is the latest start minus the earliest start. For C: 17 minus 10 is 7 days. For A, B and D, total float is zero; they are the critical path, A to B to D, 45 days. A one-day slip on any of them is a one-day slip in completion. Utilities can slip up to 7 days and nothing happens to the finish. Free float, a narrower measure, is how long an activity can slip before it delays the very next activity; in this small example it is also 7 days for C.

Say that out loud now.

The critical path is the longest chain of logic. Float is how far an activity can slip before it moves the finish. Zero float means every day counts.

Who owns the float

Here is the question that turns scheduling into money. Suppose you, the owner, are late approving the utility connection drawings by 5 days. C starts on day 15 instead of 10. Because C had 7 days of float, completion does not move. Was that free? To you, yes. But the contractor may have planned to use that float himself, for example to absorb bad weather. If you consumed it, his buffer is gone.

Contracts answer the question in different ways, all of them commercial and legal choices, not standards. Some say float belongs to the project and is available to whichever party needs it first. Some reserve it to the contractor. Some say it belongs to the owner. Some share it. The choice changes who pays for delay, and it must be written into the contract, because the default position varies between legal systems; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Day 4 takes this through the clauses.

Baseline, look-ahead and the Last Planner System

The baseline schedule is the accepted plan against which progress is measured. It is a reference, not a forecast: you update the forecast monthly, but you keep the baseline unchanged, so you can see the slippage. A baseline is only useful if it has been reviewed for quality: every activity has a predecessor and a successor, there are no artificial date constraints holding activities in place, durations are realistic, and the critical path makes sense.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A contractor submits a 900-activity baseline showing completion in month 22. Petra's review finds 140 activities with no successor, meaning their delay would never show up as a delay to anything, and 30 activities pinned to fixed dates by constraints. Remove the constraints and connect the open ends, and the network shows completion in month 24. The month-22 date was not a plan. It was a typed number. The time to find that out is at baseline review, not in month 20.

Below the baseline sits the look-ahead: a detailed plan of the next three to six weeks, prepared by the people who will do the work. The Last Planner System, developed in the 1990s by Glenn Ballard and Greg Howell and promoted by the Lean Construction Institute, formalises this: the foremen and trade supervisors commit weekly to work they can actually do, after removing constraints such as missing drawings, materials or access; the team measures the percentage of commitments kept each week, called percent plan complete; and they record why the misses happened. It turns the schedule from a document the contractor's scheduler produces into a set of promises the crews make to each other.

How the best do it

Disciplined general contractors run a constraint log alongside every look-ahead: each activity in the next six weeks is checked for design, materials, labour, equipment, access, permits and preceding work, and nothing enters the weekly plan until its constraints are cleared. A small developer cannot run the contractor's schedule, but he can ask to see the constraint log every week, because the owner's own constraints, drawings, decisions and approvals, always appear in it.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: the dates of substantial completion and when an asset is available for use can affect when depreciation or similar allowances begin; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: delay drives liquidated damages and claims, so a sound baseline protects both parties. Banking: lenders size interest reserves and maturities on the schedule; a weak baseline means a weak loan. Governance: baseline acceptance and any change to it should sit in the authority matrix. Estate: a project with a clear, logic-driven schedule can be taken over and finished by others. Exit: the completion date sets the refinancing or sale date, so float protects the exit.

Professional sign-off required: a qualified scheduling professional, on the review of the baseline schedule.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting a baseline that looks complete but has broken logic, so the schedule cannot show you a delay until it is too late. The control is an independent baseline review for open ends, constraints and unrealistic durations before acceptance.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the finish date and the bar chart, and never asks for the logic. A bar chart without logic is a drawing of hopes.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught the outside view: compare your plan with the record of similar projects before trusting it. Baseline review is the outside view applied to durations: if the network says the structure takes 60 days and comparable buildings took 90, the logic may be sound and the duration still wrong.

Recap

The critical path method models logic, runs a forward and backward pass, and finds the longest chain. Float is how far an activity can slip without moving the finish, and the contract must say who owns it. The baseline is the reviewed reference plan; the look-ahead and the Last Planner System turn it into weekly commitments.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: a composite case of a baseline that hid its own delay.
checklist: I ask for the logic network, not just the bar chart.
I know which activities are on the critical path and their total float.
The contract states who owns float.
The baseline is independently reviewed for open ends, constraints and durations before acceptance.
I keep the accepted baseline unchanged and compare each monthly update against it.
I see the contractor's three- to six-week look-ahead and its constraint log every week.
My own owner decisions appear in the constraint log with dates needed.
head: Field checklist
speak: A schedule is a model of logic. The critical path method links activities by the order they must happen, runs a forward pass to find the earliest dates and a backward pass to find the latest, and identifies the longest chain, the critical path, which sets the finish. In my small example, excavation, foundations and the slab form a 45-day critical path, and utilities have 7 days of total float. Float is how far an activity can slip before it moves completion, and the contract must say who owns it, because using float shifts who pays for delay. The baseline is the accepted reference plan, and it must be reviewed before acceptance for open ends, artificial date constraints and unrealistic durations, or its finish date is just a typed number. Below it sit the look-ahead and the Last Planner System, where the crews make weekly commitments after constraints are cleared.
terms: Critical path — the longest chain of logically linked activities through a schedule, which determines the earliest possible finish.
Total float — the time an activity can slip without delaying the project's completion.
Baseline schedule — the reviewed and accepted plan against which progress and delay are measured.

hostile.q: Your consultant rejected my baseline for 140 open ends. The dates are right. Why are you holding up acceptance?
hostile.a: Because with 140 activities that have no successor, a delay to any of them would never show up as a delay to completion, so neither of us could measure progress or claims honestly. When we connected them and removed the fixed-date constraints, the network showed month 24, not month 22. Send a revised baseline with complete logic, and if your durations support month 22, I will accept month 22.

title: The Baseline That Hid Its Own Delay: A Composite
summary: In this composite case, a baseline accepted without review, monthly updates that reported dates but not float, and a resequencing that spent the float turned a six-month financing margin into a loan extension and a late refinancing. Ford and Roman take it through seven steps. Rule 50 makes logic review and float reporting non-negotiable.
body:
This is a composite example. The project was never late on paper until it was very late in fact, because its baseline was built to show a date rather than to model the work, and the float was spent before anyone noticed it existed.

Recall

Q. What is free float?

A. The time an activity can slip before it delays the very next activity, as distinct from total float, which is measured against project completion.

Q. What does Rule 49 say?

A. No design change is accepted until the designer responsible has re-analysed it in writing; any change to structure or life safety goes through change control and is logged with its analysis.

Q. What is a time bar?

A. A notice provision under which a claim for money or time is lost if notice is not given within the stated period.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this case is a composite: it combines patterns that recur in schedule failures, with hypothetical round numbers, and no real project or company is described. Roman joins Ford because a schedule failure is, in the end, a financing failure. The building gets finished. The money runs out first.

Step 1: Timeline

A developer builds a 120-unit rental building. The construction loan matures at month 30, leaving six months after the planned completion at month 24 for lease-up and refinancing. The contractor submits a baseline showing completion at month 23. The owner accepts it within a week. Monthly updates report "on schedule" until month 16. At month 18, the forecast moves to month 26. At month 22, to month 29. The building reaches substantial completion at month 30. The lender extends the loan for a fee and a rate increase, requires additional equity to top up the interest reserve, and takes a cash sweep until refinancing. The refinancing closes at month 38 on less favourable terms than the pro forma assumed.

Step 2: Key decisions

Four decisions shaped the outcome. Accepting the baseline in a week without a logic review. Accepting monthly updates that showed the finish date without showing float on the critical path. Allowing the contractor to resequence the envelope in month 12 to "recover time," which consumed the float on the path to the interior finishes. And, in month 18, choosing to wait and see rather than to fund acceleration, because the contractor said he would recover.

Step 3: Assumptions

The owner assumed a schedule from an experienced contractor was a sound model. He assumed "on schedule" meant the finish was secure, when it only meant the finish date had not yet been changed. He assumed float was something the contractor would protect. And he assumed six months between completion and maturity was a generous margin; it was, until 6 months of delay used every day of it.

Step 4: Incentives

The contractor wanted the contract and a competitive finish date helped win it. Once on site, reporting a slip early invited questions about his own performance, so the incentive was to resequence quietly and hope. The owner's project manager was judged on keeping the job moving, not on the quality of the schedule. The lender's monitor reported the dates the schedule showed. Nobody was paid to find bad news early, and the one person who carried the cost, the owner, had no independent view.

Roman adds the lender's incentive. The lender's monitor was engaged to confirm progress against the schedule it was given, not to audit the schedule's logic, and the loan documents did not require a reviewed baseline as a condition of first draw. So the lender, too, measured time against a number nobody had tested. A small developer can turn that around: ask the lender to make an independently reviewed baseline a condition precedent, because it costs little and both of you benefit from a measure you can trust.

Say that out loud now.

"On schedule" only means the finish date has not yet been changed. Float tells me whether it is still true.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The signs were there from the start. The baseline had many activities with no successor and several pinned to fixed dates. The structure's duration was shorter than comparable buildings took. Percent plan complete on the weekly look-ahead, where it was measured at all, fell steadily from month 8. The month-12 resequencing was described as recovery, but the critical path's total float dropped from 25 working days to 5 in one update. Each of these was visible in documents the owner already received.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return came around month 18. With the float gone and the finish at month 26, acceleration, meaning extra crews, overtime or resequencing paid by the owner, could still have recovered most of the time at a known price. After month 20, the remaining work was interior trades in a fixed sequence, floor by floor, where more people would mostly get in each other's way. From then on the delay could be managed, not recovered.

Notice that the window for a cheap decision closed months before the delay became obvious. That is the general shape of schedule failures: the forecast date moves late, while the float that would have warned you moves early. An owner who watches float acts in the window; one who watches the date acts after it.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was an owner who had no independent measure of time. The baseline was accepted without review, so it could not reveal delay. Float was never reported, so its consumption was invisible. And the financing was sized on the contractor's date, with no buffer tied to the quality of that date. The delay itself had ordinary causes: optimistic durations and a lost sequence. The failure was that nobody could see it until it could no longer be fixed.

Roman's note: what the delay did to the money

A worked example, hypothetical. Six months of delay at a time-related cost of about 300,000 dollars a month is 1,800,000 dollars. Add an extension fee of 1 percent on a 30,000,000 dollar loan, 300,000 dollars, a higher rate for the extension period, and the cost of refinancing eight months later than planned in a market that had moved. On 10,000,000 dollars of equity, that is easily a fifth of the equity consumed by time alone, before counting any construction overrun. A second calculation shows the cost of the alternative: acceleration at month 18 priced at 900,000 dollars to recover four months, against four months of carry at 300,000 dollars, 1,200,000 dollars, plus the protection of the loan maturity. The decision to wait cost more than the decision to pay.

Professional sign-off required: a qualified scheduling professional, on baseline review and delay analysis; lawyer, on extension and default provisions in the loan.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is measuring time only by the finish date the contractor reports. The control is an independent baseline review before acceptance and a monthly report of total float on the critical path, with a trigger when it falls.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hears "we will recover" and waits. Recovery is a plan with resources and dates, or it is a hope.

Callback

In Week 45, Nadia and Priya taught the maturity gap between the construction loan and the take-out. This case shows how the gap is consumed: not by the market, but by a schedule that hid its own delay until the gap was gone.

Recap

A baseline accepted without review, updates that reported dates but not float, a resequencing that spent the float, and a decision to wait turned a six-month margin into a loan extension and a late, costlier refinancing. Rule 50: I never accept a baseline that has not been reviewed for logic, and I report total float on the critical path every month, with a trigger to act when it falls.

Next: Priya, on The Money: what a day of delay costs, and when acceleration is the cheaper choice.
checklist: No baseline is accepted until it has been independently reviewed for logic.
Every monthly update reports total float on the critical path.
I have a trigger level of float that forces a recovery plan.
Any resequencing is reported with its effect on float before I accept it.
I track percent plan complete on the weekly look-ahead.
I size the financing margin on the quality of the schedule, not just its date.
I compare the cost of acceleration with the cost of carry before deciding to wait.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case. A developer accepted a contractor's baseline in a week without a logic review. Monthly updates said on schedule until month 16, but they reported dates, not float. In month 12 the contractor resequenced the envelope to recover time and the critical path's float fell from 25 working days to 5. At month 18 the finish moved to month 26 and the owner chose to wait. The building finished at month 30, exactly at loan maturity, so the lender extended for a fee and a higher rate and demanded more equity. On hypothetical numbers, time alone consumed a fifth of the equity, and acceleration at month 18 would have been cheaper than the carry. My rule, Rule 50: I never accept a baseline that has not been reviewed for logic, and I report total float on the critical path every month, with a trigger that forces a recovery decision when it falls.
terms: Acceleration — adding resources, shifts or resequencing to finish sooner than the current forecast, usually at extra cost.
Percent plan complete — the share of weekly work commitments actually completed, a measure of planning reliability.
Cash sweep — a loan term that directs surplus cash to the lender until a condition, such as refinancing, is met.

hostile.q: You report the project on schedule, but your float on the critical path has dropped from 25 days to 5 in one month. Why should I believe the finish date?
hostile.a: You should not rely on the date alone, and neither do I. Our trigger is 10 days, so the drop has already forced a recovery review. The contractor is producing a recovery schedule with resources by Friday, our scheduler will test its logic, and I will bring you the recovery plan, the cost of acceleration against the cost of carry, and the effect on maturity, before the next draw.

rule: Rule 50: I never accept a baseline that has not been reviewed for logic, and I report total float on the critical path every month, with a trigger that forces a recovery decision when it falls.

title: What a Week Costs, and When to Pay to Get It Back
summary: Priya prices delay in three currencies, cash carry, deferred income and financing risk, on a hypothetical project. She shows why liquidated damages rarely cover the full loss, how to compare acceleration with carry, and how time hurts the return twice.
body:
Time on a development is priced in three currencies at once: cash carry, lost revenue and financing risk. Once you can put a dollar figure on a week, you can decide rationally whether to wait, recover, or pay to accelerate.

Recall

Q. What does Rule 50 say?

A. I never accept a baseline that has not been reviewed for logic, and I report total float on the critical path every month, with a trigger that forces a recovery decision when it falls.

Q. What is the cost of a scope gap bought after award?

A. Its tender value plus layered markup, bond and insurance, disruption and, if on the critical path, time-related cost; it can approach twice the tender value.

Q. What is the recourse spectrum in project finance?

A. The range from full recourse, where sponsors guarantee the debt, to limited recourse, where lenders look mainly to the project's assets and cash flows, with defined guarantees in between.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Week 48 priced the cost of a slow owner decision. Today Priya widens the lens to the whole schedule: what time does to the loan, to the return, and to your options. The key move is this: a delay is not a cost to be absorbed, it is a cost to be compared, with the cost of preventing it.

The three currencies of time

In plain English, a late project costs you money now, delays money later, and puts the loan itself at risk.

The first currency is cash carry: interest, the contractor's general conditions and your own team, paid every month the project stays open. The second is deferred revenue: net operating income (NOI), the income left after operating costs, that arrives later, which lowers the internal rate of return (IRR), the annual return that discounts all the cash flows to zero. The third is financing risk: delay brings the completion date closer to the loan's maturity, and an extension, if it can be had at all, costs fees, a higher rate and often extra equity.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A 30,000,000 dollar project, with a 21,000,000 dollar loan at 8 percent, nearly fully drawn at the end. Interest: 21,000,000 times 8 percent divided by 12 is 140,000 dollars a month. General conditions: 90,000 dollars a month. Owner's team: 30,000 dollars a month. Cash carry: 260,000 dollars a month, about 60,000 dollars a week. Expected stabilised NOI is 2,400,000 dollars a year, 200,000 dollars a month deferred. So each month of delay costs 260,000 dollars of cash and defers 200,000 dollars of income.

Liquidated damages: the contract's own price for time

Many construction contracts contain liquidated damages: a fixed amount per day or week the contractor pays if he finishes late through his own fault, agreed in advance as a genuine estimate of the owner's loss. The amount and any cap are commercial terms, negotiated; how courts treat a sum that looks like a penalty rather than an estimate depends on the governing law, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Two cautions. First, liquidated damages rarely cover your full loss: a contractor will resist a rate as high as your true daily cost, and caps commonly limit the total. Second, they are usually your exclusive remedy for delay, so a low rate caps your recovery. In our example, suppose liquidated damages are set at 5,000 dollars a calendar day, about 150,000 dollars a month, against a cash carry of 260,000 dollars plus deferred income. Even when the contractor is fully at fault, you carry the difference.

Say that out loud now.

Each month late costs about 260,000 dollars of cash on this project. Liquidated damages may return 150,000. The rest is mine.

Acceleration against carry

Once delay is priced, the acceleration decision is arithmetic plus judgment. A second worked example, hypothetical. At month 16 the forecast shows completion two months late. The contractor offers to recover six weeks by running a second shift on drywall and finishes, at a price of 350,000 dollars. Six weeks of cash carry at about 60,000 dollars a week is 360,000 dollars, plus six weeks of deferred NOI at about 46,000 dollars a week, roughly 276,000 dollars. On cash alone, acceleration roughly breaks even. Counting deferred income it is clearly cheaper. And there is a third value: the loan matures at month 30, and recovering six weeks restores margin before maturity, which is worth more than its carry if the market is tightening. You would also check two risks: that second-shift productivity is real, and that the extra cost does not push the loan out of balance. Acceleration paid by the owner should be agreed as a change, with milestones the contractor must hit to be paid in full.

What time does to the return

Time hurts IRR twice: it raises the cost, lowering profit, and it stretches the period, so the same profit is earned over more years. A simple illustration: an equity investment that doubles in three years earns an IRR of about 26 percent a year; the same doubling over four years earns about 19 percent. A year's delay, with no change in profit, takes about a quarter of the annual return. That is why investors who see a project slip ask about time before they ask about cost.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, delay is a liquidity event before it is a profit event. Equity is first in and last out, so a late project keeps your capital locked longer, may call for a top-up to the interest reserve, and can trigger guarantees of completion or carry. If your personal liquidity floor, the reserve you keep untouched, is already thin, a six-month delay can force you to sell something else at a bad time. Size your own reserves against a plausible delay on every project you sponsor, not against the contractor's date. Conceptual only; a licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

Monthly thread: time and energy on a rotating shift schedule

A schedule has a critical path; so does your week. On a rotating shift pattern, the hours after a run of nights are poor hours for reading a baseline or signing a change, because attention and judgment dip with sleep debt, a well-established finding in sleep research. Map your own week the way Petra maps a project: mark the decision windows where you are rested, and put the critical owner tasks, schedule reviews, negotiations, approvals, there.

Protect those windows the way you protect float. When a contractor wants a decision during your post-night recovery, the answer can be "you will have it by Thursday at noon," which is both honest and fast enough. General guidance only; check with your doctor about sleep and shift work.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is waiting on a slipping schedule because acceleration has an invoice and delay does not. The control is to price a week of delay on every monthly report and compare it with any recovery option before deciding.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes liquidated damages protect him from delay. They usually cover part of the loss, are often capped, and do not help at all when the delay is his own.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage taught that IRR is sensitive to timing as well as amount. Today's illustration, a doubling over three years against four, is that lesson in construction form: the schedule is a timing assumption in the return.

Recap

Time costs cash carry, deferred income and financing risk. Liquidated damages are the contract's partial price for contractor delay. Price a week of delay, compare it with acceleration, and remember that time hurts the return twice, through cost and through duration.

Next: LEX, on The Rules: baseline acceptance, float ownership and extensions of time.
checklist: I know the project's cash carry per week and deferred NOI per week.
I know the liquidated damages rate and cap, and the gap between them and my true loss.
Every monthly report prices a week of delay.
I compare any recovery or acceleration offer with the carry it saves.
Owner-paid acceleration is agreed as a change with milestones.
I check that acceleration does not push the loan out of balance.
I size my personal liquidity floor against a plausible delay, not the contractor's date.
I schedule my own critical decisions into rested windows.
head: Field checklist
speak: Time costs me in three currencies: cash carry, deferred income and financing risk. On a hypothetical 30,000,000 dollar project, cash carry is about 260,000 dollars a month, and each month late defers about 200,000 dollars of income, while bringing completion closer to the loan's maturity. Liquidated damages are the contract's fixed price for contractor delay, but they are usually lower than my true loss and often capped, so I carry the difference. When a project slips, I compare acceleration with carry: an offer to recover six weeks for 350,000 dollars roughly matches six weeks of cash carry and is clearly cheaper once deferred income and maturity risk are counted. Time also hurts the return twice: doubling money over four years instead of three takes the annual return from about 26 percent to about 19. So every monthly report prices a week of delay.
terms: Liquidated damages — a fixed sum per day or week, agreed in the contract as an estimate of the owner's loss, payable when the contractor finishes late through its own fault.
Cash carry — the cash cost of keeping a project open each month, such as interest, general conditions and owner's staff.
Extension fee — a fee a lender charges to extend a loan beyond its original maturity.

hostile.q: Why should I pay 350,000 dollars to accelerate when your liquidated damages already compensate you for delay?
hostile.a: Because they do not, and that is not a criticism of you. Our liquidated damages are about 150,000 dollars a month and capped, against cash carry of 260,000 dollars a month plus deferred income and a loan that matures at month 30. Six weeks recovered is worth more to me than 350,000 dollars, provided the milestones are real. I will pay it as a change, in stages tied to the recovered milestones.

title: Schedule Clauses: Acceptance, Float and Extensions of Time
summary: LEX explains the clauses that make a schedule a legal instrument: baseline submission and what acceptance means, monthly updates as evidence, float ownership and why it flips who pays, and extensions of time with their notice and analysis requirements.
body:
A schedule becomes a legal instrument through a handful of clauses: when the baseline must be submitted and what acceptance means, how often it is updated, who owns float, and how an extension of time is claimed and granted.

Recall

Q. What are liquidated damages?

A. A fixed sum per day or week, agreed in the contract as an estimate of the owner's loss, payable when the contractor finishes late through its own fault.

Q. What is the valuation ladder in a change clause?

A. Contract unit rates first, then rates derived from them, then an agreed lump sum, and failing those, actual cost plus a stated markup.

Q. What is actual authority?

A. The power a principal really gives an agent, expressly or by reasonable implication.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every delay dispute on a project eventually turns on the schedule clauses: what the baseline was, whether it was accepted, who was entitled to the float, and whether notice was given in time. This lesson teaches the concepts those clauses contain. It is not a jurisdictional conclusion. Contracts differ and courts differ, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it, and have your lawyer read the actual clauses.

Baseline submission and the meaning of acceptance

In plain English: the contract usually requires the contractor to submit a detailed schedule soon after award, and the owner to respond to it.

The clause typically sets a deadline for submission, the level of detail, the software or format, and what the schedule must show, such as logic, durations and resources. It then says what the owner's response means. This is the critical point. If the owner "approves" the schedule, he may be taken to agree that the durations and sequence are achievable, which can make the owner share responsibility if they are not. Many owners therefore "accept" or "note" the schedule instead, with words saying that acceptance does not relieve the contractor of responsibility for its adequacy. Whether that distinction holds depends on the contract and the law. The wording matters less than consistency: use the same response on every submission, and never write anything that sounds like confirmation that the plan is achievable. A worked example, hypothetical: an owner writes "approved" on a baseline that shows an impossible structure cycle. When the structure runs late, the contractor argues the owner endorsed the plan. Had the owner written "accepted as the baseline for measuring progress; acceptance does not confirm the durations or sequence," that argument is much weaker.

Updates and the as-planned versus as-built record

The clause should require updates at a fixed interval, usually monthly, with actual start and finish dates, remaining durations, and a narrative explaining changes to logic and the critical path. It should forbid changing the baseline without the owner's agreement. The point is evidence: delay analysis compares what was planned with what happened, and both records must exist and be trustworthy. An update that silently changes logic to hide delay destroys that evidence.

Two drafting points help the owner. First, require the contractor to submit the native schedule file, not only a printed or image version, so your scheduler can test the logic rather than look at bars. Second, require every update to list each change to logic, durations and constraints since the last update, with the reason. A worked example, hypothetical: in month 9 the contractor shortens the remaining drywall durations from 60 to 40 working days without explanation, and the forecast finish holds. With a change list, your scheduler sees the cut in the same week and asks for the crew plan that supports it. Without one, the cut is invisible until month 14, when drywall is late and the shortened durations have quietly become the new reference.

Float ownership

Here the law and the drafting meet. Absent clear words, systems differ on who may use float, and the answer can decide who pays for delay. The common drafting choices are: float belongs to the project, available on a first-come basis; float is shared; or float belongs to one party. Some forms and guidance documents, including the Society of Construction Law's Delay and Disruption Protocol in the United Kingdom, discuss these approaches [unverified — confirm independently].

A second worked example, hypothetical. A non-critical activity has 15 working days of float. The owner's late design information delays it by 10 days. Under a "float belongs to the project" clause, completion is not affected, so the contractor gets no extension of time; the float absorbed the owner's delay. Later, the contractor's own subcontractor is late by 10 days on the same path. With only 5 days of float left, completion slips 5 days, and the contractor bears it. Under a clause reserving float to the contractor, the first event would entitle the contractor to recover the lost float, and the outcome flips. Same events, opposite money.

Say that out loud now.

Who owns float decides who pays for delay. The contract must say it, in words.

Extensions of time and notice

An extension of time is a contractual adjustment of the completion date for delays the contract says the contractor is not responsible for, such as owner-caused delay or, in many forms, defined events like unusual weather. Its purpose cuts both ways: it protects the contractor from liquidated damages for delay he did not cause, and it protects the owner's right to liquidated damages, because in many systems an owner who causes delay but has no mechanism to extend time may lose the right to liquidated damages altogether, sometimes called the prevention principle [unverified — confirm independently].

The clause sets notice requirements: written notice within a stated time of the event, followed by particulars, usually supported by a time impact analysis, which inserts the delay event into the current schedule to show its effect on completion. As with changes, notice may be a condition precedent. Whether delay is merely excusable, meaning time but no money, or also compensable, meaning time and money, and how concurrent delay from both parties is treated, are larger topics that return in Week 118.

For the owner, the practical lesson about extensions is to grant them on time, when they are due, rather than to refuse them as a negotiating stance. An owner who refuses a justified extension may find that, if the dispute is later decided against him, the contractor was entitled to treat the original date as gone, with consequences for liquidated damages that depend on the law; this is a question for your lawyer. An extension granted promptly, against a proper analysis, keeps the completion date and the liquidated damages meaningful.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on the schedule, float, extension and liquidated damages clauses and the governing law; a qualified scheduling professional, on the specification of baseline and update requirements.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an owner who approves a baseline he has not reviewed and leaves float ownership unstated, so the first serious delay becomes a dispute over what the plan was and who had the slack. The control is clear drafting before award: accept rather than approve, state float ownership, require monthly updates with narratives, and set notice and analysis requirements.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks an extension of time is a concession to the contractor. It is also the mechanism that keeps the owner's liquidated damages enforceable.

Callback

Last week, LEX taught that a change clause is first about authority and notice, and only then about price. Schedule clauses work the same way: the dates matter less than who accepted the plan, who owns the float, and whether notice was given in time.

Recap

Schedule clauses set baseline submission and what acceptance means, monthly updates that preserve the record, who owns float, and how extensions of time are noticed and analysed. Accept rather than approve, state float ownership in words, and treat the extension mechanism as protection for both sides.

Next: Petra, on The Numbers: working a schedule backward from the date the loan needs.
checklist: The contract sets a deadline, detail and format for the baseline.
I accept the baseline as a measuring tool rather than approving its durations.
Monthly updates must include actuals, remaining durations and a narrative.
The baseline cannot be changed without my agreement.
Float ownership is stated in words in the contract.
Extension of time requires written notice and a time impact analysis.
My lawyer has reviewed the schedule, float, extension and liquidated damages clauses.
head: Field checklist
speak: A schedule becomes legal through a few clauses. The contract sets when the baseline is submitted and in what detail, and what the owner's response means. I accept a baseline as the tool for measuring progress, with words that acceptance does not confirm its durations, rather than approving it, which can make me share responsibility for an impossible plan. Monthly updates must show actuals, remaining durations and a narrative, and the baseline cannot change without my agreement, because both records are evidence. Float ownership must be stated in words: belonging to the project, shared or reserved, and the same events can produce opposite payments depending on that choice. An extension of time adjusts the completion date for delay the contractor did not cause, which protects him from liquidated damages and protects my right to them. Notice and a time impact analysis are usually required, and the law differs by place.
terms: Extension of time — a contractual adjustment of the completion date for delay the contract does not put on the contractor.
Time impact analysis — inserting a delay event into the current schedule to measure its effect on completion.
Float ownership clause — contract wording that states which party, or the project, may use the schedule's float.

hostile.q: You wrote 'accepted' on our baseline, not 'approved'. Are you trying to avoid responsibility for the plan?
hostile.a: I am trying to put responsibility where the contract puts it. The plan is yours, because you control the means and methods. Acceptance means we both use it to measure progress and delay, and I have reviewed its logic so it can do that honestly. If the plan turns out to need changing, the contract's update and extension provisions apply to both of us.

title: Working the Schedule Backward From the Loan
summary: Petra starts from the date the financing needs, a hypothetical month-30 loan maturity, and works backward through lease-up, commissioning and the podium to a required floor cycle. She compares the contractor's planned cycle with the reference class, checks the finishing trades, and turns the risk into three decisions.
body:
The most useful schedule calculation starts at the end. Take the date the loan and the lease-up need, work backward through the work, and you find the production rates the building must achieve, and whether the contractor's plan has any float left to protect them.

Recall

Q. What does an extension of time protect for the owner?

A. The right to liquidated damages, because in many systems an owner who causes delay without an extension mechanism may lose that right.

Q. What is total float?

A. The time an activity can slip without delaying the project's completion.

Q. What is the in-balance test?

A. Undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity must cover the full cost to complete; any shortfall is deposited before the next draw.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an even-numbered week, so we reverse engineer. Instead of building a schedule forward from the start, we start from the finished outcome you need, a completion date the financing can live with, and work backward to what the site must do every week. This is the calculation that tells you, before you sign, whether a contractor's date is ambitious, realistic or impossible. All figures are hypothetical round numbers, in working days of five per week unless stated.

Step 1: The date the money needs

The construction loan matures at month 30. The permanent lender will refinance only after the building reaches a stated occupancy, which your lease-up plan says takes six months from substantial completion. You want a further two months of margin for refinancing to close. Working backward: maturity at month 30, less 2 months of margin, less 6 months of lease-up, gives a required substantial completion of month 22. That is the outcome. Everything else is worked back from it.

Step 2: Subtract the fixed end and start

The building is eight residential floors over a podium. Construction starts at month 1. From the end: commissioning, inspections and the occupancy approval take 8 weeks after the last floor's finishes are complete. From the start: site works, excavation and foundations take 16 weeks, and the podium takes 12 weeks. So the time available for the superstructure and the interior work above the podium is from week 28, after 16 plus 12 weeks, to month 22 less 8 weeks. Month 22 is about week 95. Less 8 weeks is week 87. The window is 87 minus 28, which is 59 weeks.

Step 3: Split the window into structure and finishes

The upper floors are built in a repeating sequence: structure, then envelope, then rough-in services, then finishes, with each trade following the one ahead floor by floor. The last floor's finishes end the window. If the finishes on one floor take 10 weeks from the start of rough-in, then the last floor's structure must be complete roughly 10 weeks before week 87, plus the envelope lag. Suppose the envelope closes a floor 4 weeks after its structure. Then the structure must finish by week 87 minus 10 minus 4, which is week 73.

The structure starts at week 28 and must finish by week 73: 45 weeks for eight floors, plus the roof. Treat the roof as one more floor-cycle. Nine cycles in 45 weeks is 5 weeks per cycle, or 25 working days per floor.

Say that out loud now.

Maturity at month 30 means completion at month 22, which means the structure must cycle a floor every 25 working days, with nothing to spare.

Step 4: Compare with the contractor's plan and the outside view

The contractor's baseline shows a structure cycle of 15 working days per floor. On its own logic that finishes the structure in 9 times 15, 135 working days, 27 weeks, ending at week 55 instead of week 73. Between the required cycle and the planned cycle there are 18 weeks of float on the structure path. That looks comfortable.

Now apply the outside view from Week 2. Ask what comparable cast-in-place buildings in your market have actually achieved. Suppose your cost consultant's records show 20 to 30 working days per floor for buildings of this type. At 20 days, the structure finishes at week 64, with 9 weeks of float. At 30 days, it finishes at week 82, which is 9 weeks past the week-73 limit, and completion moves to about month 24, two months into your refinancing margin. The 15-day cycle is not impossible, but it is outside the reference class, and the plan's comfort depends on it.

Step 5: Convert the risk into decisions

Reverse engineering ends with choices, all of them commercial practice rather than standards. Three follow from this one.

  1. Ask the contractor to show how he achieves 15 days: crew sizes, formwork system, crane capacity, concrete supply and curing. If it rests on a system such as table forms or a second crane, check those are in his price.
  2. Set a trigger: if the first three floor cycles average more than 20 working days, the contractor produces a recovery plan and you review the financing margin.
  3. Re-size the financing to the outside view, not the baseline. If a 25-day cycle is realistic, either negotiate a longer loan term or an extension option at the outset, when it is cheap, or carry more interest reserve.

A second worked check: the finishes

The same backward logic applies to the trades that follow. If each finishing trade needs 2 weeks per floor and the crew can only work one floor at a time, eight floors take 16 weeks for that trade alone. With five finishing trades following each other with a one-week offset, the last trade finishes 16 plus 4 weeks after the first trade starts, 20 weeks, against the 10 weeks per floor assumed in Step 3 for a single floor. The plan only works if each trade runs two floors at once, which needs double crews. Check that the contractor's resource plan shows them; if it does not, the finishes, not the structure, are the real critical path.

Notice what the two checks together tell you. The structure has float on the contractor's plan but little on the reference class, and the finishes may have none at all unless the crews double. A schedule can look comfortable on its most visible activity and be fragile on the work behind it. Reverse engineering from the date the money needs exposes both, because it forces every stage to fit inside one fixed window. Repeat the backward pass whenever the lease-up assumption or the loan terms change, because each one moves the required completion date, and with it every rate you derived from it.

Professional sign-off required: a qualified scheduling professional, on the baseline and the production assumptions; quantity surveyor, on whether the methods that support them are priced.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting the contractor's production rate because it produces a comfortable float, without testing it against what comparable buildings achieved. The control is to work backward from the financing date to a required rate, compare the planned rate with the reference class, and set an early trigger on the first cycles.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner works forward from the contractor's start date and admires the finish. Work backward from the date the money needs, and the questions that matter appear on their own.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage reverse engineered a deal from public information to an implied land price. Today is the same move applied to time: from a known outcome, the date the financing requires, back to the implied production rate the site must achieve.

Recap

Start from the maturity, subtract margin and lease-up to find required completion, subtract the fixed start and end, and divide the window into structure and finishes to get a required floor cycle. Compare the plan's cycle with the reference class, check the following trades' resources, set a trigger on the first cycles, and size the financing to the realistic rate.

Next: Petra, on The Room: the baseline review meeting with the contractor's scheduler.
checklist: I start from loan maturity and subtract margin and lease-up to find required completion.
I subtract the fixed start and end durations to find the working window.
I convert the window into a required production rate per floor.
I compare the contractor's planned rate with what comparable buildings achieved.
I check that the methods and resources behind the planned rate are priced.
I check the finishing trades' crew plan, not only the structure.
I set a trigger on the first three cycles.
I size the loan term, extension option or reserve to the realistic rate.
head: Field checklist
speak: I reverse engineer the schedule from the date the money needs. The loan matures at month 30. Less two months of refinancing margin and six months of lease-up, completion must be month 22. Less eight weeks of commissioning at the end and 28 weeks of site works, foundations and podium at the start, the upper floors have a 59-week window. Allowing ten weeks of finishes and four weeks of envelope behind the last floor, the structure must finish by week 73: nine cycles in 45 weeks, a floor every 25 working days. The contractor plans 15, which looks like 18 weeks of float, but comparable buildings achieved 20 to 30 days. At 30, completion slips to about month 24. So I ask how 15 days is achieved and priced, I set a trigger if the first three cycles exceed 20 days, I check the finishing trades have double crews, and I size the financing to the realistic rate.
terms: Floor cycle — the working days needed to complete one repeating floor of structure before starting the next.
Production rate — the quantity of work a crew or system completes per unit of time, such as floors per month.
Reference class — a set of comparable completed projects used to test a plan's assumptions.

hostile.q: Your schedule needs a 15-day floor cycle to show any real float. What makes you think you'll hit it when buildings like this usually take 20 to 30?
hostile.a: You are right that 15 days is ambitious, and I have not relied on it. I asked the contractor to show the crews, formwork system and crane plan behind it, and those are in his price. We have a trigger after the first three floors at 20 days, and the financing is sized to a 25-day cycle, with an extension option negotiated at closing. If the cycle slips, the plan changes before the maturity is at risk.

title: The Baseline Review Meeting
summary: Three weeks after award, the contractor wants his baseline accepted today. Petra walks the room: the question behind the request, how to ask about logic rather than dates, why connected logic protects the contractor too, when silence works, and how to protect his cash flow with a fast review instead of a weak acceptance.
body:
The baseline review meeting is where you decide whether the schedule will be a measuring tool or a marketing document. Ask about logic, not dates, and let the contractor's scheduler show you how the plan works.

Recall

Q. What is a floor cycle?

A. The working days needed to complete one repeating floor of structure before starting the next.

Q. Why do owners accept rather than approve a baseline?

A. Because approval may be taken as agreeing the durations and sequence are achievable, while acceptance uses the schedule to measure progress without confirming its adequacy; the effect depends on the contract and law.

Q. What is a cumulative cap?

A. A limit on the total value of decisions one person may approve, in addition to the limit on any single decision.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, contractors' schedulers are skilled and often proud of their work. A baseline review can go two ways: an adversarial audit that leaves them defensive and the schedule unchanged, or a working session that leaves both sides with a plan they believe. The difference is mostly in how you ask.

The scene

A hypothetical scene. Three weeks after award. In the room: you, Petra as your scheduling reviewer, your owner's project manager, the contractor's project manager and his scheduler, who has the baseline on a screen. Petra has sent a short written review two days earlier: 140 activities without successors, 30 date constraints, a 15-working-day floor cycle against a reference class of 20 to 30, and no resource loading on the finishing trades. The contractor's project manager opens: "We've built dozens of these. The date is the date. We'd like acceptance today so we can bill against it."

The question behind the question

"Acceptance today" means several things. He wants a baseline accepted before its weaknesses are fixed, because an accepted baseline with a short duration makes later extensions look larger and his performance look better early. He may want to avoid showing how much float he has, because float he reveals is float the owner may use. And he wants to know whether this owner's review is real or ceremonial. Underneath, he also has a legitimate interest: the contract may tie payment or milestones to an accepted schedule, and delay in acceptance can hurt his cash flow.

The lines to say

"We want to accept it, and quickly. We need a schedule both of us can use to measure progress and delay, and right now it cannot do that, for four reasons in Petra's note. Can your scheduler walk us through the structure cycle first?"

When the scheduler explains the 15-day cycle: "That's helpful. What would the cycle be if the second crane is late, or if concrete deliveries are limited to mornings? I'm not doubting the plan, I'm asking where it's fragile."

On the open ends: "When these 140 activities have a successor, their delays will show up properly, for you as much as for us. If the owner causes a delay to one of them, you'll want the schedule to prove it."

And to close: "If you can send the revised baseline by the 15th with the logic connected and the finishing crews loaded, we'll turn the review round in five working days. If the durations then support month 22, we'll accept month 22."

Say that out loud now.

Connected logic protects you as much as me. If we delay you, the schedule must be able to prove it.

The lines never to say

Never say "your schedule is wrong." Say what it cannot do yet. Never say "we'll accept it now and fix it later"; once accepted, a baseline is the reference for every claim. Never say "just give us a date we can rely on," which invites a date without logic. Never claim the float as the owner's in the meeting if the contract does not say so; that is a drafting question, not a negotiating line. And never accept a baseline because billing pressure makes the room uncomfortable; offer a fast review time instead.

When to stay silent

After asking the scheduler how the plan works, stay silent and let him talk. A scheduler explaining his own logic will often find the weak points himself: "this assumes the second crane arrives in month 3," "this one we tied to a date because the utility hadn't confirmed." Each of those sentences is worth more than any criticism you could offer. When the project manager pushes for acceptance today, a calm silence followed by the specific timetable is more persuasive than an argument.

Holding your state

A room full of people who build schedules for a living can make an owner feel he is trespassing. Hold onto one fact: you do not need to out-schedule anyone. You need to ask four questions and insist on answers in writing. Keep your notes to Petra's four points, tick each off as it is addressed, and let her handle the technical exchanges. Your role is to decide, not to debate.

After the meeting

Within a day, your project manager confirms in writing what was agreed: the revised baseline due date, the four items to be addressed, the five-day review period, and that until acceptance progress is measured against the submitted schedule for information only. That letter matters if acceptance is later disputed. When the revised baseline arrives, Petra checks each item against the note and you accept it with the agreed wording from Day 4.

A worked example of what the revision usually shows, hypothetical. With the 140 open ends connected and the 30 constraints removed, the critical path moves from the structure to the finishing trades, because the finishes were only unloaded on paper. With double crews loaded on drywall and painting, the finish moves from month 22 to month 23. Now there is a real conversation to have: either the contractor commits the resources and a recovery of the month in his own price, or the accepted baseline shows month 23 and your financing margin is checked against it. Either answer is better than a month-22 date that could not have been met.

Monthly thread: working with advisers

Petra is an adviser, and this meeting shows the right division of labour. You set the question, the adviser does the technical work, and you make the decision. The common failure is the reverse: an owner who lets the adviser argue on his behalf in front of the counterparty, so that every technical point becomes a personal contest.

Brief your adviser before the meeting on what outcome you want, and agree who speaks to which point. Afterwards, ask her one question: what did I miss? An adviser who never tells you is either not looking or not comfortable telling you, and both are worth knowing.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting a weak baseline under billing pressure, because it becomes the reference for every later claim. The control is a written review, a fast turnaround offer, and acceptance only once the logic is connected and the resources loaded.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner argues about the finish date. The contractor controls the date; the owner should test the logic behind it.

Callback

In Week 49, Marco separated the work clock from the money clock in a scope dispute. Baseline review needs the same separation: the contractor's cash flow is urgent and you can protect it with a fast review; the acceptance decision is not urgent and must wait for logic that works.

Recap

In a baseline review, ask how the plan works, not whether the date is right. Show the contractor that connected logic protects him too, offer a fast review, refuse acceptance before the fixes, stay silent while the scheduler explains, and confirm the outcome in writing.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap, with a Red Pen drill on a monthly schedule narrative.
checklist: I send a short written baseline review before the meeting.
I ask how the plan works, not whether the date is right.
I explain that connected logic protects the contractor's delay claims as well as mine.
I never accept a baseline now and promise to fix it later.
I offer a fast, defined review period instead of yielding to billing pressure.
I stay silent while the scheduler explains his own logic.
I confirm the meeting's outcome in writing within a day.
I brief my adviser beforehand and ask her afterwards what I missed.
head: Field checklist
speak: In the baseline review meeting, the contractor wants acceptance today. I say we want to accept it quickly, but right now it cannot measure progress or delay, for four reasons in the written review: open ends, date constraints, an ambitious floor cycle and no resources on the finishes. I ask the scheduler to walk us through the structure cycle and ask where it is fragile, then I stay silent and let him find the weak points himself. I explain that connected logic protects him too, because if we delay him, the schedule must prove it. I never say his schedule is wrong, and never accept now to fix later. I offer a fast review: revised baseline by the 15th, our answer in five working days, and if the durations support month 22, we accept month 22. Afterwards my project manager confirms it all in writing, and I ask my adviser what I missed.
terms: Resource loading — assigning crews, equipment or quantities to schedule activities to test whether the planned durations are achievable.
Date constraint — a fixed start or finish date imposed on an activity, which overrides its logic and can hide delay.
Open end — an activity with no predecessor or no successor, so its delay cannot flow through the network.

hostile.q: Every day you delay accepting our baseline delays our milestone payment. Why should we bear the cost of your review?
hostile.a: You should not, and you won't. Send the revised baseline by the 15th and we will review it in five working days, which the letter will confirm. In the meantime we will process your progress payment against the submitted schedule, measured for information. What we cannot do is accept a reference plan with 140 open ends, because neither of us could prove delay against it.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 50 Review: Logic, Float and the Date the Money Needs
summary: Six questions test the critical path method, float ownership, baseline review, liquidated damages, reverse engineering a floor cycle and the Last Planner System. A Red Pen drill finds eight defects in a hypothetical schedule narrative, and a two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: the schedule is a model of logic, the float is the slack that protects completion, and the owner's job is to make sure both are honest, reported and owned in writing.

Recall

Q. What does Rule 49 say?

A. No design change is accepted until the designer responsible has re-analysed it in writing; any change to structure or life safety goes through change control and is logged with its analysis.

Q. What is the owner's charter?

A. A one-page statement of a project's purpose, scope, success measures, constraints and leader, approved by whoever holds the money.

Q. What is a change directive?

A. A written instruction to proceed with a change before price and time are agreed, valued later by a stated method, with cost records kept.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the schedule is where the owner's control system, scope and money meet the calendar. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can review a baseline, read a monthly update and challenge a recovery plan. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What do the forward and backward passes find?

Answer: The forward pass finds each activity's earliest start and finish and the project's earliest finish. The backward pass finds the latest start and finish that will not delay completion. The difference is total float, and activities with zero float form the critical path.

Question 2. Why must float ownership be written into the contract?

Answer: Because using float shifts who pays for delay, the same events can produce opposite outcomes under different float clauses, and the default position varies between legal systems.

Question 3. What does a baseline review check?

Answer: Open ends, artificial date constraints, realistic durations against the reference class, resource loading, and whether the critical path makes sense.

Question 4. Why do liquidated damages rarely protect the owner fully?

Answer: They are usually set below the owner's true daily loss, are often capped, are often the owner's exclusive remedy for delay, and do not apply to delay the owner causes.

Question 5. How do you reverse engineer a required floor cycle?

Answer: Start from loan maturity, subtract refinancing margin and lease-up to find required completion, subtract the fixed start and end durations, allow for the trades following the structure, and divide the remaining window by the number of floor cycles.

Question 6. What does the Last Planner System add to a baseline?

Answer: Weekly commitments by the people doing the work, made only after constraints are cleared, measured by percent plan complete, with reasons recorded for every miss.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Petra built a critical path network and explained float, baselines and the Last Planner System. Ford and Roman took a composite case in which an unreviewed baseline hid its own delay until the financing margin was gone, giving Rule 50. Priya priced delay in three currencies and compared acceleration with carry. LEX taught baseline acceptance, float ownership and extensions of time. Petra worked a schedule backward from the loan's maturity to a required floor cycle. Petra ran the baseline review meeting.

The Red Pen

Here is a hypothetical monthly schedule narrative. Find the defects before reading on.

Schedule Update No. 11, data date end of month 11. Completion remains forecast at month 22, as per baseline. Progress: structure on level 6, approximately on plan. Critical path: unchanged. To maintain completion, the finishing trades on levels 1 to 4 have been resequenced to run concurrently, and the logic link between drywall and flooring has been removed. Three activities have been constrained to their baseline finish dates to reflect the contractor's commitment. Owner delays: drawings for the lobby are late; an extension of time will be requested at the end of the project. Float: not reported this month due to software update.

The defects. First, "completion remains forecast at month 22, as per baseline" with no float figure is exactly the reassurance Rule 50 forbids; the narrative must report total float on the critical path, and "not reported due to software update" is not acceptable at month 11. Second, "approximately on plan" for the structure gives no measure; it should state the actual cycle against the planned cycle. Third, "critical path: unchanged" cannot be true if the finishing trades were resequenced and a logic link removed; removing the drywall to flooring link may create a false float that hides delay. Fourth, running finishes concurrently on four floors needs resources that should be shown; without them it is a paper recovery. Fifth, constraining three activities to baseline finish dates overrides the logic and stops their delay from showing, which is the open-end problem in another form. Sixth, a change to logic like this should not happen without the owner's agreement under the update clause. Seventh, "an extension of time will be requested at the end of the project" ignores the notice requirement; delay must be noticed when it happens, with a time impact analysis, or the right may be lost and the owner cannot manage the cause. Eighth, the owner's late lobby drawings are named but not dated or logged, so the owner cannot measure his own delay.

The corrected narrative would state the data date, the actual floor cycle, total float on the critical path against the trigger, every logic change with the owner's agreement and its effect, the resources behind any resequencing, no date constraints without a stated reason, and every delay event noticed with its date, cause and analysis.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a lender who asks, "How do you know this building will finish before the loan matures?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "We worked backward from your maturity. Taking off a refinancing margin and the lease-up period gave us a required completion date, and from that a required floor cycle for the structure. The contractor's plan beats that cycle, but it is faster than comparable buildings achieved, so we did not rely on it: we asked to see the crews and formwork behind it, we set a trigger after the first three floors, and we sized the loan term and reserve to a realistic cycle. Before acceptance, our scheduler reviewed the baseline for logic: no open ends, no artificial date constraints, and the finishing trades resource-loaded. The contract states who owns float and requires monthly updates with narratives and timely notice of delay. Every month we report total float on the critical path against a trigger, and a week of delay is priced in the report, so a recovery decision is made while it can still work."

Score it. Did you start from the maturity? Did you mention the reference class and the trigger? Did you describe the baseline review and float reporting? Inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is trusting a finish date that has stopped being a calculation, because logic was cut, dates were constrained or float went unreported. The control is a monthly narrative that must report float and every logic change, read against Rule 50.

The beginner's mistake

Reading the finish date first. Read the float first; the finish date is only as good as the float behind it.

Callback

In Week 48, the Auditor's Chair read a monthly report that said "on track" with no evidence. This week's schedule narrative made the same claim in scheduling language. The cure is unchanged: every claim must arrive with its source, its date and the measure behind it.

Recap

The schedule models logic; float protects completion; float ownership, acceptance and notice must be written into the contract. Price a week of delay and compare it with acceleration. Work backward from the financing date to the production rate the site must achieve. Rule 50 makes logic review and monthly float reporting non-negotiable.

Next: Quincy, with Nadia, on First Principles: estimate classes, contingency structure and the cost-to-complete forecast.
checklist: What do the forward and backward passes find?
Why must float ownership be written into the contract?
What does a baseline review check?
Why do liquidated damages rarely protect the owner fully?
How do you reverse engineer a required floor cycle?
What does the Last Planner System add to a baseline?
head: The six questions
speak: A schedule is a model of logic. The forward pass finds the earliest dates, the backward pass the latest, and the difference is total float; zero-float activities form the critical path. Float ownership must be written into the contract, because the same delays can produce opposite payments depending on who owns the slack. Before acceptance, a baseline is reviewed for open ends, date constraints, realistic durations against comparable buildings, and resource loading, and I accept it as a measuring tool rather than approving it. Delay costs cash carry, deferred income and financing risk, and liquidated damages rarely cover it all, so I compare acceleration with carry. I work backward from the loan maturity to a required floor cycle and size the financing to a realistic rate. Rule 50: no unreviewed baseline, and total float on the critical path reported every month, with a trigger that forces a recovery decision.
terms: Data date — the date up to which progress has been recorded in a schedule update; everything after it is forecast.
Logic link — a relationship between two activities, such as finish-to-start, that sets their order in the network.
Recovery schedule — a revised plan, with resources and dates, showing how lost time will be regained.

hostile.q: Your update says completion at month 22, but float isn't reported, three activities are constrained to dates and a logic link was removed. Is month 22 real?
hostile.a: I cannot tell you it is until those three things are fixed, so I will not ask you to rely on it. I have rejected the update. The contractor is restoring the logic link, removing the constraints and reporting float by Friday, and the lobby drawing delay is now logged with its date and will be noticed and analysed properly. You will have the corrected update and our float figure against the trigger before the next draw.
